Base directory for this skill: /work/.claude/skills/jigc

`jigc setup` wrote this file from jigc 1.0.0-rc.13 and owns it: re-run `jigc setup` after upgrading the binary to refresh it.

It carries the two guides that ship with that binary, one after the other — the quickstart loop, then the migration field notes. A cross-reference to `QUICKSTART.md` or `MIGRATING.md` means the matching part of this file; every other jigc document named below lives in the jigc project's own repository, not in this one, which is why none of them are links here.

# Quickstart

`jigc` is a context compiler for coding agents: a deterministic CLI that
assembles exactly the instructions and document slices an agent needs for a
task, and is the sole channel through which the agent reads and writes managed
project documents. This walks the MVP loop on a real machine —
**install → start → finalize**.

> The name is **jigc** — pronounced "jig-see" — *a jig for coding agents*: the
> jig holds the work and guides the tool so the cut lands true (settled
> 2026-07-03, `DECISIONS.md` → The name is settled). The binary is the same name.

## Install

`jigc` ships as a single binary. Install it from the workspace and put it on
your `PATH`:

```sh
cargo install --path crates/cli      # or: cargo build --release -p cli
cp target/release/jigc /usr/local/bin/   # if you built rather than installed
```

Just `jigc` — nothing else to copy. The doc↔code probe (`doc-code`) is
embedded in the binary and extracted beside it by `jigc setup` (below), so a
`cargo install` from a fresh machine is a supported install channel: no manual
probe copy, and code-anchor finalize / `jigc validate` work out of the box.

Confirm it identifies itself:

```sh
jigc --version          # → jigc <version>
```

## 1. `jigc setup` — adapter install

Run once per project, from the repo root. `setup` generates the Claude Code
adapter from the embedded profile and installs it idempotently
(`design/assistant-adapter.md` → Generated, minimal, regenerated):

```sh
jigc setup
```

It does these things:

- writes the managed bootstrap file `.jigc/AGENT.md` and adds a bare
  `@.jigc/AGENT.md` import to `CLAUDE.md` (the static floor that tells the agent
  `jigc` is its interface to the project — a plain import line, no marker fence);
- allowlists `Bash(jigc:*)` in `.claude/settings.json` and adds a `SessionStart` hook
  that runs `jigc start` (so each session opens with orientation), so the agent
  can call the CLI without a permission prompt;
- writes jigc's own guides — this file and the migration field notes — to the path
  your assistant reads skills from (`.claude/skills/jigc/SKILL.md` for Claude Code),
  as **one file jigc owns**: it opens with a `jigc-version:` stamp naming the build
  that wrote it plus the hash of its own body, and every `jigc setup` rewrites it, so
  the guidance in your repo always matches the binary in your `PATH`. Re-run `setup`
  after upgrading and the copy follows;
- extracts the embedded `doc-code` probe beside the installed `jigc` (so the
  doc↔code probe resolves next to the binary — written if no sibling is present
  **or** if an existing sibling's bytes differ from the embedded copy, so a
  stale or corrupt probe self-heals; a byte-identical sibling is left untouched); and
- installs a `pre-commit` hook that runs `jigc validate` over the committed
  store and **warns** on doc↔code drift without blocking the commit — a
  backstop for edits made outside the loop, not a gate. It refuses exactly one
  thing: a commit that itself stages an out-of-band managed-doc **rename** (a
  bare `git mv` of a managed doc, both paths staged), because that silently
  breaks identity tracking — use `jigc rename` instead. Drift that landed in an
  earlier commit only warns; it never blocks a later, unrelated one.

`setup` **commits its own install** as a dedicated
`chore(jigc): install jigc workspace config` commit, so the install doesn't land in
your first feature commit. It stages **only the files it wrote inside the repo** —
never your working tree — so two of the things above are *not* in that commit: the
`doc-code` probe (it lives beside the `jigc` binary, not in your repo), and the
`pre-commit` hook whenever git keeps hooks outside your working tree — the usual
`.git/hooks/`, a `core.hooksPath` pointing elsewhere, or a linked worktree's shared
hooks dir — because git cannot track a file there. If your repo keeps hooks *in* the
tree (an in-repo `core.hooksPath`), the hook is an ordinary tracked file and `setup`
commits it with the rest — unless git will not take that path from your repo, in which
case `setup` leaves the hook out of its commit and commits the rest normally. That
covers a hooks dir belonging to **another** repository (shared hooks vendored as a
submodule — checked out or not — or an embedded repo), where it is that repo's file to
commit, not yours, and a hooks dir your **sparse-checkout** excludes. Either way the
hook is installed and works locally, it just isn't in the commit; note that a committed
hook carries **this** machine's `jigc`
path, so in someone else's clone it stays silent until they run `jigc setup`
themselves. These edits are idempotent — re-running `jigc setup` leaves the files
byte-identical (no new commit), so it is safe to run after every upgrade to re-apply
the adapter.

## 2. `jigc start "<intent>"` — route, then mint

Hand the agent (or yourself) a task by stating the intent. `start` composes
the cascade-default **router** (`design/write-commands.md` → Task
origination): it presents the selectable work-workflows with the situation
each fits, and emits the re-run line — nothing is minted yet:

```sh
jigc start "add per-client rate limit at the gateway"
# → the workflow menu, then the re-run line:
#   jigc start --workflow <chosen> "<intent>"
```

Pick the workflow whose situation fits the intent and re-run with that
choice — this is the call that mints:

```sh
jigc start --workflow single-task "add per-client rate limit at the gateway"
```

This opens the task's working area under `.jigc/tasks/<id>/` and emits the
composed workflow — the instructions plus the document slices the task needs.
The agent reads its intent and the codebase, implements the change directly in
the working tree, and (when a decision is warranted) records an ADR in-task
through the workflow's `create` gate.

Bare `jigc start` (no intent) orients instead: it reports project state and the
next action, read-only.

### Reading while the task is open

Managed docs are read through `jigc`, never off disk — three reads cover it, and
`--task <id>` turns the first two onto the working copies your open task has
staged but not yet committed:

```sh
jigc doc list --task <id>             # what this task stages, each by its address
jigc doc show adr:<slug> --task <id>  # the staged doc itself
jigc doc schema adr                   # the shape a write has to fill
```

Drop `--task` and the first two serve the committed store instead. `jigc doc
schema` needs no task — it projects the resolved schema: required slots and
fields, each field's enum members, and every address a write can take.

## 3. `jigc task finalize <id>` — the commit boundary

When the work is done, finalize. This is the single transactional boundary
(`design/finalize.md`): it validates, renders the commit-doc into the git commit
message, promotes any created ADR into `docs/decisions/`, and `git`-commits the
code changes plus promoted docs as one commit.

```sh
jigc task finalize <id>
```

If validation blocks (a dangling forward reference, a missing required slot, a
malformed value), finalize makes no commit and surfaces the findings with a
route for the next action. Fix and re-run.

Your own `pre-commit` / `commit-msg` hooks still run — jigc never passes
`--no-verify`, they are your policy — so a hook that rejects the commit stops
the finalize. Nothing is committed, the task survives — its staged docs still in
`.jigc/tasks/<id>/docs/`, anything you had `git add`-ed still in git's index —
and the message carries the hook's own output verbatim plus the line to re-run
once its complaint is fixed. Every jigc verb that commits on
your behalf answers a rejection that way, each stating what *its* rejection
left behind — the per-door detail is in MIGRATING.md →
Reconciling and backing out.

A landed finalize prints a **manifest** — the file-set the commit carried (the
git index: what you staged plus the docs jigc promotes), with a distinct
**left-out** list naming any unstaged or untracked work the commit excluded (so
a stray `scratch.txt` stands out as left behind, never swept in). To see that
set *before* committing, run `jigc task finalize <id> --dry-run`: it prints the
manifest and stops, changing nothing. A change staged *before* the task existed
refuses to ride the commit (`finalize.carried-staged`) unless you declare it
with `--carry-staged`.

Changed your mind? **`jigc task discard <id>`** abandons the task — it removes
only the working area under `.jigc/tasks/`; no commit is made and the committed
store is untouched. The full reconcile/back-out ladder (the migration review
hold, the carryover gate, the hook rejection above, out-of-band edits) is in
MIGRATING.md → Reconciling and backing out.

**What lands in your repo:** finalize promotes each managed doc under the
**`docs-root`** parent (default `docs/`) at its doctype's location —
`docs/decisions/` (ADRs), `docs/specs/`, `docs/prds/`, `docs/architecture/`
(arch-docs), `docs/milestone-records/` — as plain, human-reviewable Markdown
alongside your own `src/`. (The names are chosen for readability, not a uniform
`<type>s/` rule.) A few doctypes are **placed** rather than located: they live at
one literal path that `docs-root` does not move — the changelog is your
repo-root `CHANGELOG.md` (design/storage.md → Placement).
Prefer a different parent, or the old flat repo-root layout? Set
`jigc config set docs-root <path>` (`.` or `""` for the old flat layout). Everything else jigc
writes lives under `.jigc/` (committed config + bootstrap; gitignored caches) —
see design/storage.md → Repository layout / Config layout. If
you already have a same-named dir (say an existing `docs/architecture/`), run
`jigc ingest` first — it detects and routes existing content rather than
overwriting it.

You can preview part of what finalize will gate on at any time — this task's
content findings, the carryover gate, the `owner-artifact` causes that need no
staging, and the granted-but-unused changelog gate. The staged set, promotion
and the commit itself (your hooks included) are decided at `finalize`, so a clean `validate` means *nothing this
side of the commit blocks it*, not *this will commit*:

```sh
jigc task validate <id>
jigc task diff <id>
```

---

That is the whole loop: **`jigc setup`** once, then **`jigc start "<intent>"` →
pick from the menu → `jigc start --workflow <chosen> "<intent>"` → implement →
`jigc task finalize <id>`** per task. See
`design/worked-examples.md` for end-to-end flows
and `implementation/roadmap.md` for the build
sequence.
# Migrating to jigc — field notes

Two different migrations get called "migrating to jigc." Both have now been run for real on a brownfield repo (the RC adoption trial, 2026-07-09 → 07-12); these notes distill what worked and what bites. They are working notes, not polished docs — updated as trials land.

1. **Adopting an existing project** — foreign docs (a `.planning/` tree, loose Markdown, an old spec system) become jigc-managed docs. Verb: `jigc ingest` to classify, `jigc migrate <path> --as <doctype>` per doc.
2. **Upgrading a jigc corpus across versions** — committed managed docs move to a new doctype schema-version. Verb: `jigc migrate-corpus`.

## Adopting an existing project

The full method write-up from the reference migration (220 foreign files → 41 managed docs, ~55 commits, one day) is archived at completions/artifacts/RC-adoption/rerun-rc4/migration-method.md. The short version:

1. **Triage with the tool first.** `jigc ingest` classifies every candidate against the managed schemas before you decide anything. Conformant-but-misplaced docs can be adopted; everything else is a re-authoring job through the write verbs. Knowing the split up front sets the whole plan's cost.
2. **Treat every claim in the old docs as unverified.** This is the load-bearing rule, and it is why adoption is a *verification* job, not a reformatting job. Your existing docs may already be lying about the code — status claims especially ("shipped", "passes audit", "the gate works"). Check each claim against the code before carrying it over; a false claim migrated into jigc is *worse* than a deleted one, because the new system lends it credibility (managed, validated, green). Don't migrate what you haven't verified — and where a claim can't be cheaply verified, either drop it or carry it explicitly marked as unverified and put the verification question to the human.
3. **Mine history for the four things worth keeping:** design decisions whose rationale isn't recoverable from the code, still-open debt, architecture knowledge, and work claimed complete that the code doesn't support. Everything else (plan summaries, validation reports, velocity tables) is process exhaust — drop it.
4. **Put the genuine forks to the human** — not "should I proceed" but the actual decisions (delete vs mine-then-delete, is this doc still live, where does the backlog land).
5. **Draft in parallel, write strictly sequentially.** Prose drafting and code-verification parallelize. Since rc.8 the *draft/author* half of bulk migration parallelizes even for docs sharing a directory: two same-directory sources whose slugs would collide today mint **distinct** task ids (a `blake3` of each source path is folded into the migration task id), so their `.jigc/tasks/<id>/` working areas no longer race the tool state. The jigc *writes* still run strictly sequentially — the git-index race is unchanged, each doc mints its own commit, so the finalize/commit path is one process, never parallel.
6. **Author in dependency order.** Cross-referencing docs must land after their targets: ADRs before the arch-docs that cite them — finalize blocks a citation to a doc that doesn't exist.
7. **Let `jigc migrate` retire each source in the same commit as its promoted doc.** The old tree drains itself; there is never a window where content exists in neither place. Then sweep for what the migration broke *outside* the corpus (READMEs pointing at the deleted tree, a stale CLAUDE.md).
8. **Prefer block scalars (`key: |`) in author payloads** for any multi-paragraph prose (the templates demonstrate this since rc.5; double-quoted YAML folds newlines).

## Upgrading a jigc corpus across versions

Verified on the first real committed-corpus upgrade (rc.4 → rc.5, a 41-doc corpus, one doctype with an enum rename across 41 entries — byte-stable, zero prose touched, idempotent re-run). That trial found the *routing* around the upgrade silent, so the rc.6 wave hardened it; the steps below are the shipped surface.

1. **Ask `jigc validate` whether you need to migrate — it blocks if you do.** A committed doc below its doctype's current schema-version raises `schema-conformance.schema-version-current`, routed at `jigc migrate-corpus`, and takes the exit code **non-zero**. The discriminator is each doc's own committed `schema-version` stamp, so the answer never depends on when the store was last stamped.
2. **Run `jigc migrate-corpus` first, `jigc setup` second — and the tool now says so.** Over a stale corpus the `store-version.binary-mismatch` advisory routes at `migrate-corpus` first, and re-stamping the store no longer buys a green: `validate` still blocks on the per-doc stamps. Re-stamp with `jigc setup` once the corpus is current (with the corpus current, the advisory drops `migrate-corpus` from its route). *(Before rc.6 the ordering was yours to enforce — a re-stamped store over an unmigrated corpus validated clean.)*
3. **Look first: `jigc migrate-corpus --dry-run`** prints the triage report the run *would* produce and changes nothing — no migrated bytes, no relocation move, no commit. Run the real thing on a clean tree, so the diff is the whole story.
4. **The run lands its own commit.** `migrate-corpus` writes the migration and commits it, pathspec-limited to the paths it migrated (a half-landed migration — rewritten docs beside a removed relocation source, only some of them staged — is the failure mode that closes). `--no-commit` keeps the writes in the working tree instead, to review them or fold them into a larger commit yourself.
5. **Audit what landed.** The transform is deterministic and the triage (`migrated` / `already_current` / `blocked` in `--format json`) tells you exactly what moved; the line accounting should close exactly (every changed line either a `schema-version` stamp or a declared transform). `blocked` docs are first-class output — they need a human or a prose rewrite, never a workaround.

## Reconciling and backing out

Nothing in either migration is destructive until you say so. The gates, in the order you meet them (each verified against the shipped binary):

1. **Look before landing: `jigc task finalize <id> --dry-run`.** It prints the manifest the finalize *would* commit — each path tagged by how it enters (`promoted` / `modified` / `deleted` / `carried-over`) — and stops. 5. **A rejecting hook refuses the commit, and the message says how to recover.** jigc never passes `--no-verify` — your `pre-commit`/`commit-msg` hooks are policy — so a hook that exits non-zero stops the run and **nothing was committed** (HEAD does not move). What comes back is the hook's own stderr **verbatim**, a sentence naming what survived, and the exact line to re-run: fix the hook's complaint, run that line, and the commit lands. What survives differs per door and the message states *that door's* truth — `jigc task finalize <id>` leaves the task intact — its staged docs still in `.jigc/tasks/<id>/docs/`, anything you had `git add`-ed still in git's index, HEAD unmoved (the message names the two areas separately, because a docs-only task has nothing in git's index for you to check); `jigc migrate-corpus` leaves the migrated bytes written and staged, and its re-run **lands** them instead of reporting "already current"; a rejected `jigc milestone create` unwound both its record write and its workbench, so nothing of that milestone survives. All nine committing doors carry the frame, each with its own error code in the invocation log, so a failed run is identifiable afterwards.
6. **Back out a task: `jigc task discard <id>`.** Workbench-only — it removes the task's working area (`.jigc/tasks/<id>/`) and touches nothing else: no commit, the committed store exactly as it was. A migration task discarded before `--approve` leaves the foreign source committed and untouched — abandoning costs nothing.
7. **Back out a milestone: `jigc milestone discard <id>`.** The committed milestone record settles to `status: discarded` in one record-only commit — a genuinely joined sub-task stays `joined`; it really did land — and then the workbench (sub-task areas, fan-out worktrees) tears down. A sub-task worktree holding uncommitted work refuses the discard unless `--force`.
8. **Hand edits are detected and routed — never silently merged, never forbidden.** Editing a committed managed doc outside the loop is expected (it is plain Markdown in git). `jigc validate` names the drifted path with a route to re-author it through the owning workflow; the report is exit-0 at store scope and gates at `jigc task validate` / `jigc task finalize`.

## What migration does *not* give you

- **Truthful prose.** jigc's gates keep docs naming *real code* (anchors, refs, structure); they do not detect that a paragraph's *claim* went stale. A migrated corpus is only as honest as the verification you did at step 2 above — and it starts rotting again the first time a fix lands without its doc pass.
- **Linear-time authoring of a very large document.** Every `migrate-*` workflow hands `jigc doc author` the whole document in **one** payload, and the apply chain re-reads the growing buffer once per lowered leaf — so the cost is **quadratic in the item count**, not linear, and that residual is the shipped bound. That factor is gone — the same 800-item document now takes under 7 s, 1500 items under 30 s — but quadratic is still quadratic: a single source document with several thousand items is minutes, not seconds. The batch is atomic, so a long run is a long run and never a partial one; if a foreign document is enormous, splitting it at a real boundary beats waiting.

- **A finished doc set.** Migration carries what exists. The gaps the old system had (undocumented decisions, missing specs) are still gaps — now visible ones.

# Reject the newest sample when the ingest queue is full

## Context

`IngestQueue` is a bounded FIFO between the wire and the store, sized by a
capacity given at construction. Under sustained pressure — a burst of writers,
or a store that has stopped draining — the buffer reaches capacity and the queue
has to shed something. There is no third option: the process either refuses the
write it is being handed, or it discards something it is already holding.

The two behaviours are not equivalent for the consumers downstream. A rollup
buffer exists to answer "what is happening now"; every sample it holds is there
to be aggregated into a recent window. So the question is not which sample is
cheapest to lose, but which loss leaves the window most wrong.

## Options

**Refuse the incoming sample.** The buffer keeps everything it already has and
the writer is told its sample did not land. Back-pressure is explicit and the
writer can decide what to do. The cost is that the window freezes: under
sustained pressure the aggregate keeps reporting the oldest capacity-worth of
samples, and a consumer reading "now" is reading the past with no signal that
this is happening.

**Discard the oldest buffered sample.** The incoming sample always lands and the
buffer sheds from the far end. The window stays current; the loss is silent
unless the queue reports it, which is why a dropped counter is kept alongside.

## Decision

**Drop the oldest sample.** On overflow the queue evicts from the front of the
buffer and accepts the incoming sample, incrementing a `dropped` counter so the
loss is observable rather than invisible.

Under sustained pressure a recent picture beats a stale one: this service is a
bounded in-memory buffer over a recent window, and a window that has stopped
advancing is worse than a window with a hole in it. Refusing the newest sample
would preserve data that no consumer of a "recent window" asked for, at the cost
of the only data they did.

## Consequences

The `dropped` counter becomes load-bearing: it is the only signal that the
window is lossy, so it must be surfaced wherever queue health is reported, and a
non-zero value must not be treated as routine.

Writers get no back-pressure from the queue, so a writer that outruns the drain
indefinitely will never be told. If back-pressure is wanted later it has to come
from somewhere other than the overflow path — a depth check before the write,
not a refusal at capacity.

Replay and audit are out of scope for this buffer by construction. Anything that
needs every sample must read from the durable store, not from here.

# Drop the oldest sample when the ingest queue overflows

## Context

`IngestQueue` is a bounded FIFO between the wire and the store, sized by a
capacity given at construction. Under sustained pressure — a burst of writers,
or a store that has stopped draining — the buffer reaches capacity and the queue
has to shed something. There is no third option: the process either refuses the
write it is being handed, or it discards something it is already holding.

The two behaviours are not equivalent for the consumers downstream. A rollup
buffer exists to answer "what is happening now"; every sample it holds is there
to be aggregated into a recent window. So the question is not which sample is
cheapest to lose, but which loss leaves the window most wrong.

Research task (not code, not jigc actions — just investigate and report back).

Context: I'm about to write a jigc `research` doc (slots: question, findings, sources) about a design gap in this repo's `MemoryStore` (src/store.ts): it's a `Map<string, Sample[]>` keyed by series name, with `maxSamples` bounding samples *per series*, but nothing bounds the number of distinct series (map keys). A single runaway label (e.g. a series name derived from unbounded user input, or a UUID/timestamp accidentally embedded in a series name) grows the map unboundedly and can OOM the process. This is the classic "cardinality explosion" problem in time-series/metrics systems.

Do web research (use WebSearch/WebFetch) on how comparable real-world systems handle unbounded label/series cardinality, and what it costs them operationally. I want concrete, citable specifics — not generic "cardinality is bad" content. Cover at least:

1. **Prometheus** — `sample_limit` in scrape configs, any series/label limits, and the well-documented OOM failure mode from cardinality explosions. What's the actual mechanism (reject whole scrape vs. drop samples) and its cost/tradeoff?
2. **Cortex/Mimir (Grafana)** — per-tenant active series limits (e.g. `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` or Mimir's equivalent), what happens when the limit is hit (429s to the client?), and what that costs (dropped writes, tenant needs to request limit increase, etc).
3. **VictoriaMetrics** — `-storage.maxHourlySeries` / `-storage.maxDailySeries` flags, what they do when hit, and the tradeoff.
4. **InfluxDB** — the classic "series cardinality" failure mode (in-memory index per series), any `max-series-per-database` / `max-values-per-tag` limits in 1.x, and what happens when hit.
5. **Datadog or another SaaS metrics vendor** — cardinality-based billing / "custom metrics" limits as a *cost-based* rather than technical bound (e.g. Datadog's "Metrics without Limits").

For each, note: (a) the actual bounding mechanism, (b) what happens to the write/series that exceeds it (reject new series? evict old? drop samples? bill more?), (c) what it costs operationally or financially, (d) a real citable source (official docs, engineering blog, or well-known incident writeup) with URL.

Also note the general design-pattern takeaway across these systems: is there a common shape to how they bound cardinality (e.g., a hard cap on distinct series count, enforced at write time, with new series beyond the cap rejected while existing ones keep flowing — as opposed to LRU-evicting old series to make room)?

Report back in plain text (no file writes, no jigc calls) as:
- A "findings" section: 4-6 tight paragraphs I can adapt almost verbatim into the research doc's findings slot — concrete, specific, with mechanism/cost per system, then the cross-system takeaway.
- A "sources" section: a plain list of `[Title](URL) — one-line note on what it supports`, one per source actually used.

Keep total findings prose to roughly 400-600 words — dense and specific, not padded.

## Findings

**Prometheus** bounds cardinality at scrape time with the `sample_limit` field in a scrape config, disabled by default. It is a hard, coarse-grained cap: if a single scrape returns more time series than the limit, Prometheus rejects the *entire* scrape as failed (target `up=0`) rather than truncating or sampling — a deliberate all-or-nothing choice, described by Prometheus experts as an "emergency release valve," not a fix. This avoids partial/inconsistent ingestion but means one runaway label (e.g., a metric with a user-ID label) can blackout an entire target's metrics until the underlying label is fixed via `metric_relabel_configs` or the offending metric is dropped. The unbounded case — no `sample_limit` set — is the classic OOMKilled failure mode: cardinality grows monotonically in Prometheus's in-memory head block until the process is killed, which is exactly the crash scenario the researched `MemoryStore` risks.

**Grafana Mimir/Cortex** enforce cardinality centrally and per-tenant rather than per-scrape. `-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` (and the related per-ingester `max_series`) caps active series per tenant across the cluster. The two limits fail differently: hitting the per-ingester instance limit is a 5xx server error — new-series writes fail but samples on *existing* series keep flowing, and clients retry — whereas hitting the tenant-global limit is treated as a 4xx client error, meaning the excess write is discarded outright with no retry/data-loss protection. Either way the pattern is the same shape: existing series are never evicted to make room; only *new* series beyond the cap are rejected. Operationally, the fix is either identifying and cutting the high-cardinality tenant/label or an operator manually raising the runtime-config limit — i.e., a human-in-the-loop cost/capacity decision, not automatic eviction.

**VictoriaMetrics** uses `-storage.maxHourlySeries` and `-storage.maxDailySeries` on `vmstorage` to cap unique active series within a rolling hour/day window (the latter specifically targeting high "churn rate" — series that appear and disappear rapidly, which is exactly what a UUID/timestamp-embedded label produces). When the cap is hit, new series beyond the limit are rejected/logged and not admitted to storage, while already-tracked series continue to be written. It's a pure admission-control gate, not an eviction policy — nothing pre-existing is deleted to free budget for new series.

**InfluxDB (1.x)** is the canonical cautionary tale: its TSI/in-memory series index means every unique series consumes index memory that scales with cardinality, and tag values like unique IDs, hashes, or accidental timestamps-as-tags are the textbook cause of unbounded growth and OOM. InfluxData's own config exposed `max-series-per-database` (historically defaulting around 1,000,000) and `max-values-per-tag` (default 100,000) as hard admission caps: once hit, InfluxDB refuses to write the *new* series/tag-value and returns a "partial write" error for that point, while writes to already-existing series/tag-values keep succeeding. Operators have documented (e.g., GitHub issue #10409) that this enforcement was historically buggy — cardinality could exceed the configured cap under certain interactions between the two limits — reinforcing that this class of protection is easy to get subtly wrong, not just "add a counter."

**Datadog**, as a SaaS vendor, takes a fundamentally different, economic approach: rather than capping cardinality technically, it prices it. Every unique metric-name + tag-value combination is a billable "custom metric," so cardinality explosions show up as invoice spikes, not crashes. Its mitigation, "Metrics without Limits," decouples *ingestion* (everything is always accepted) from *indexing/billing* (only an admin-curated allowlist/blocklist of tags stays queryable and billable) — turning the cardinality problem into a configuration/cost-governance problem rather than a memory-safety one.

None of them LRU-evict old series to admit new ones; eviction-to-make-room is conspicuously absent from all four, presumably because silently deleting a live series' data is worse than refusing a new one. The only SaaS example (Datadog) sidesteps the crash risk entirely by making unindexed cardinality cheap-to-ingest but expensive-to-query, shifting the bound from a memory ceiling to a billing signal. `MemoryStore` (`src/store.ts`) keys an in-memory `Map<string, Sample[]>` by
series name, and `maxSamples` bounds the depth of each per-series bucket —
but nothing bounds the number of distinct keys the map can hold. A single
runaway label (a series name that embeds a user id, a UUID, or a timestamp)
grows the map without limit until the process runs out of memory.

How do comparable time-series and metrics systems bound unbounded
label/series cardinality, and what does that bound cost them — operationally
or financially — once it is in place?
EOF

jigc doc set-slot research:how-comparable-systems-bound-unbounded#findings --from-file - --task investigate-how-comparable-time-series --format json <<'EOF'
**Prometheus** bounds cardinality at scrape time with the `sample_limit`
field in a scrape config, disabled by default. It is a hard, coarse-grained
cap: if a single scrape returns more time series than the limit, Prometheus
rejects the *entire* scrape as failed (target `up=0`) rather than truncating
or sampling — a deliberate all-or-nothing choice, described by Prometheus
experts as an "emergency release valve," not a fix. This avoids
partial/inconsistent ingestion but means one runaway label can blackout an
entire target's metrics until the offending metric is relabeled or dropped.
The unbounded case — no `sample_limit` set — is the classic OOMKilled
failure mode: cardinality grows monotonically in Prometheus's in-memory head
block until the process is killed, exactly the crash scenario `MemoryStore`
risks today.

**Grafana Mimir/Cortex** enforce cardinality centrally and per-tenant.
`-ingester.max-global-series-per-user` (and the related per-ingester
`max_series`) caps active series per tenant across the cluster. The two
limits fail differently: hitting the per-ingester limit is a 5xx — new-series
writes fail but samples on *existing* series keep flowing, and clients
retry — whereas hitting the tenant-global limit is a 4xx, so the excess write
is discarded outright with no retry. Either way, existing series are never
evicted to make room; only *new* series beyond the cap are rejected.
Operationally the fix is a human decision: cut the high-cardinality label, or
an operator raises the runtime-config limit.

**VictoriaMetrics** uses `-storage.maxHourlySeries` and
`-storage.maxDailySeries` on `vmstorage` to cap unique active series within a
rolling hour/day window — the daily one specifically targets high "churn
rate," which is exactly what a UUID/timestamp-embedded label produces. When
the cap is hit, new series beyond the limit are rejected/logged and not
admitted to storage, while already-tracked series continue to be written: a
pure admission-control gate, not an eviction policy.

**InfluxDB (1.x)** is the canonical cautionary tale: its in-memory series
index means every unique series consumes index memory that scales with
cardinality, and tag values like unique ids, hashes, or accidental
timestamps-as-tags are the textbook cause of unbounded growth and OOM.
InfluxData exposed `max-series-per-database` (historically defaulting around
1,000,000) and `max-values-per-tag` (default 100,000) as hard admission
caps: once hit, InfluxDB refuses to write the *new* series/tag-value and
returns a partial-write error for that point, while writes to
already-existing series/tag-values keep succeeding. Operators have
documented that this enforcement was historically buggy — cardinality could
exceed the configured cap under certain interactions between the two
limits — a reminder that this class of protection is easy to get subtly
wrong, not just "add a counter."

**Datadog**, as a SaaS vendor, takes a different, economic approach: rather
than capping cardinality technically, it prices it. Every unique
metric-name + tag-value combination is a billable "custom metric," so
cardinality explosions show up as invoice spikes, not crashes. Its
mitigation, "Metrics without Limits," decouples ingestion (everything is
always accepted) from indexing/billing (only an admin-curated allowlist of
tags stays queryable and billable) — turning the cardinality problem into a
cost-governance problem rather than a memory-safety one.

**Cross-system takeaway.** Every self-hosted system here converges on the
same shape: a hard cap on distinct-series count enforced at write/admission
time, where series beyond the cap are rejected (or the whole batch is
rejected, Prometheus-style) while series already tracked keep flowing
uninterrupted. None of them LRU-evict old series to admit new ones —
silently deleting a live series' data is worse than refusing a new one. The
only SaaS example (Datadog) sidesteps the crash risk entirely by making
unindexed cardinality cheap to ingest but expensive to query, shifting the
bound from a memory ceiling to a billing signal. The directly transferable
pattern for `MemoryStore` is: track distinct series count, and once a
`maxSeries` cap is reached, reject/drop samples for *new* series names while
continuing to accept samples for series already in the map — never evict an
existing series to make room for a new one.
EOF

**We are betting that the label space stays operator-bounded, and are not
adding a series-count cap yet.** `MemoryStore` keeps accepting a sample for
any series name that reaches it, with no limit on how many distinct series
it will track.

This is a conscious bet, not an oversight: today's only ingest path hands
series names straight from hand-authored wire lines, and every series this
service has ever seen in practice is a small, fixed, operator-defined label
set. Under that assumption the map's width is bounded by the number of
metrics the operators define — effectively static — so the crash mode the
research describes has no trigger yet. Building the admission cap now, before
there is a caller that could actually blow the space up, would be capacity
management for a problem this deployment does not currently have.

The bet is scoped, not indefinite: it holds only as long as every series
name reaching `MemoryStore` is operator-chosen. The moment a series name is
ever derived, even indirectly, from something with unbounded range —
end-user input, a request id, a UUID — the bet is off and the cap described
in `docs/research/how-comparable-systems-bound-unbounded.md` (reject
samples for new series once a `maxSeries` cap is hit, never evict an
existing series) is the documented, ready-to-build fallback.

## Consequences

Nothing in `MemoryStore` changes today. `maxSamples` still bounds each
series' depth; nothing bounds how many series exist.

If the bet holds, this costs nothing: an operator-sized, static label set
never approaches a memory problem worth guarding against.

If the bet breaks — a series name ever starts carrying unbounded-range data —
the failure mode is exactly the one the research documents: unbounded map
growth ending in an OOM kill, with no admission control to contain it and no
graceful degradation on the way there. Nothing in the code currently detects
that this is happening; there is no series-count metric or alert to catch it
before the crash.

Any future ingest path that accepts series names from a less trusted or
less bounded source (a public write API, a multi-tenant caller, labels that
embed request- or user-scoped data) must not inherit this bet silently — it
should add the `maxSeries` admission cap described above before going live,
not after the first incident. This ADR is the trigger to re-open that
decision when such a path is proposed.
